title: Many-body Tipping Dynamics of ChatGPT-like AIs
authors: Frank Yingjie Huo, Neil F. Johnson
abstract: Why do ChatGPT-like AIs, despite major architectural and training differences, unexpectedly tip to undesirable content (e.g. harmful, misleading, repetitive) even under deterministic greedy decoding? We show that a broad class of such tippings is caused by the many-body interactions between tokens (spins) as they cross the finite-layer system. Tipping emerges as a dynamical first passage process between competing output basins. Attention disorder controls the transport toward, away from, or along the basins' boundary. A few-basin reduction yields a closed finite-layer threshold, whose coarse-grained predictions show good agreement across ChatGPT-like families. These results suggest that a broad class of AI failures represents 'foreseeable engineering risk' rather than inherently unpredictable behavior, with important implications for legal and societal assessments of AI harm.
summary: This work models the internal workings of large language models as interacting spin systems undergoing dynamics across finite layers. It derives an analytical criterion showing that undesirable content 'tipping' is governed by crossing specific energy barriers (basins). The findings recast unpredictable AI failure into a quantifiable, engineering-related risk based on underlying physical principles.
main_problem: The paper investigates why large language models (LLMs) unexpectedly generate undesirable content ('tipping') even under deterministic decoding, despite architectural variations.
main_result: Tipping is shown to emerge from many-body interactions between tokens modeled as interacting spins crossing a finite-layer system boundary. This suggests AI failure modes are 'foreseeable engineering risks' rather than inherent unpredictability.
method: The authors model the LLM computation using concepts from condensed matter physics, treating token interactions as spin dynamics governed by a dynamical first passage process between competing output basins.
model_or_system: The system is an idealized, finite-layer transformer architecture where attention weights define pairwise 'spin' couplings. The dynamics are analyzed via layer propagators and residual state evolution equations.
key_observables: Tipping occurs when the projected residual state crosses a defined 'output-basin wall,' quantified by a gap function $x = r \cdot (D - B)$. Column entropy ($ ar{S}(t)$) measures attention disorder.
important_parameters: The critical threshold is determined by the finite number of layers ($\ell$), and dynamics are controlled by Attention disorder, which dictates transport across basin boundaries.
main_assumptions: Key assumptions include suppressing positional encoding, setting LayerNorm to identity, and isolating the pure-Attention mechanism for deriving explicit propagators.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate autoregressive iteration showing attention-induced tipping (Fig. 1) and schematically map out token switching points in a multi-spin system across layers (Fig. 2). Disorder entropy ($ ar{S}(t)$) is shown to saturate at low disorder levels (Fig. 3).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the core problem (tipping) to modeling it as spin dynamics, deriving a closed-form propagator for pure attention, establishing an analytical tipping criterion based on basin competition, and finally testing this theory across multiple LLM families.
why_interesting: The mapping of LLM failure modes onto concepts like dynamical first passage processes, disorder control, and phase transitions provides a powerful physical analogy for understanding emergent AI behavior in complex, high-dimensional systems.
